questions.q: Using the lesson's example, what is the ROI of a $10,000 campaign linked to $45,000 of won opportunities?
questions.explain: (45,000 - 10,000) / 10,000 = 3.5, or 350 percent. These are example numbers.

questions.q: Actual Cost is blank on half of your campaigns. What is the correct way to treat their ROI?
options: Treat it as zero cost, giving infinite ROI
Treat it as undefined, filter to campaigns with a cost, and say so on the report
Fill the blanks with the average cost
questions.explain: ROI cannot be computed without cost. Excluding those campaigns and stating it is honest; guessing values is not.

questions.q: Why might a campaign that ran last month show zero won value?
options: ROI cannot be calculated for recent campaigns
Revenue lags spend, so its deals may not have closed yet within the sales cycle
Won opportunities are hidden for 90 days
questions.explain: Sales cycles mean revenue trails spend. Report young campaigns as pipeline, or compare only campaigns older than a full cycle.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of the standard native attribution model?
options: It credits one campaign per opportunity (the primary source), so other touches get no credit
It splits credit equally across every campaign ever run
questions.explain: Single-source credit hides multi-touch influence. Campaign Influence, where enabled, can spread credit using a chosen model.

questions.q: What should you confirm before comparing campaign numbers if Campaign Influence might be in use?
options: Whether the report is a matrix
Whether the campaign has a parent
Whether it is enabled and which influence model is used
questions.explain: The influence model changes how revenue is credited to campaigns, so it changes every ROI number that depends on it.
